stem: Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act 1932 defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed to share:
options: the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all
the ownership of a property purchased jointly by all of them for their own use
the capital of a business managed by any one of them acting for all the others
the receipts of a charitable activity carried on by all or any of them for all
explanation: Correct option: (A). Section 4 defines partnership as the relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all. Joint ownership of property is co-ownership, not partnership. Sharing capital is not the test; sharing profits of a business is. A charitable activity is not a business carried on for profit, so it is not a partnership.

stem: In which of the following situations does a partnership exist?
options: Two friends jointly buy a plot of land and hold it together as co-owners
Five persons pool their money to run a free blood donation camp every year
Two persons regularly buy and sell plots of land and share the profit
A trader employs a manager who is paid only a fixed monthly salary
explanation: Correct option: (C). A partnership needs an agreement to carry on a business and share its profits. Buying and selling land for profit and sharing that profit is a business carried on together. Mere co-ownership of land does not amount to partnership. A free blood donation camp is a charitable activity with no profit to share. A manager on a fixed salary is an employee who does not share profits.

stem:
Assertion (A): The private assets of a partner can be used to pay off the debts of the firm.
Reason (R): The liability of a partner for the acts of the firm is unlimited.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both statements are true. Because a partner's liability for the acts of the firm is unlimited (and joint and several), creditors of the firm can recover their dues from the partner's private assets when the firm's assets are not enough. The Reason therefore directly explains the Assertion.

stem: Neha, Om and Pia agree to share the profits of a shop. Under their agreement only Neha may act for the shop; her acts do not bind Om and Pia, and they cannot act for the shop at all. Which essential feature of partnership is missing here, without which the textbook says there would be no partnership?
explanation: Correct option: (D). Each partner must be a principal as well as an agent of the others, able to bind them and be bound by their acts in the firm's business. Here Neha's acts do not bind Om and Pia and they cannot act for the shop, so the relationship of mutual agency is absent, and without it there is no partnership. Profits are shared, there is an agreement among the three, and running a shop is a business, so those features are present.

stem: Ravi and Sonu are partners with capitals of Rs. 3,00,000 and Rs. 1,00,000. Their deed is silent on all matters. Sonu advanced a loan of Rs. 50,000 to the firm on October 1, 2025. The profit for the year ended March 31, 2026, before any interest, is Rs. 60,000. Ravi claims interest on capital at 10 per cent and Sonu claims a salary. The total amount credited to Sonu for the year is:
explanation: Correct option: (D). Only the loan interest is allowed when the deed is silent: 50,000 x 6/100 x 6/12 = Rs. 1,500, a charge against profit. Neither interest on capital nor salary is allowed. Remaining profit = 60,000 - 1,500 = Rs. 58,500, shared equally, so Sonu gets 29,250. Total = 29,250 + 1,500 = Rs. 30,750. Rs. 31,500 charges loan interest for a full year (3,000 + 28,500). Rs. 30,000 ignores the loan interest. Rs. 16,125 wrongly shares profit in the capital ratio 3:1 (58,500 x 1/4 + 1,500).

stem: Under the fixed capital method, a partner's share of profit, interest on capital and drawings are recorded in the partner's:
explanation: Correct option: (A). Under the fixed capital method, the capital account records only the capital introduced or permanently withdrawn; all other items such as share of profit, interest on capital, salary, drawings and interest on drawings go to a separate Partner's Current Account. Recording them in the capital account is the fluctuating capital method. A loan account records loans, and no drawings suspense account is used.

stem: When there is no instruction about the method of maintaining partners' capital accounts, they should be prepared by the:
explanation: Correct option: (B). In the absence of any instruction, partners' capital accounts are prepared by the fluctuating capital method, with all adjustments recorded directly in the capital accounts. The fixed capital method, under which a capital account and a current account are kept for each partner, is used only when the partners agree to it. stem: Under the fixed capital method, Tara's current account had an opening credit balance of Rs. 10,000. During the year: share of profit Rs. 30,000, interest on capital Rs. 6,000, drawings Rs. 50,000 and interest on drawings Rs. 1,500. Her current account at the end of the year will show:
options: a credit balance of Rs. 5,500, shown on the liabilities side
a debit balance of Rs. 2,500, shown on the assets side
a debit balance of Rs. 5,500, shown on the assets side
a debit balance of Rs. 15,500, shown on the assets side
explanation: Correct option: (C). Credits: 10,000 + 30,000 + 6,000 = Rs. 46,000. Debits: 50,000 + 1,500 = Rs. 51,500. Debits exceed credits by Rs. 5,500, so there is a debit balance, which goes to the assets side of the balance sheet. Rs. 2,500 wrongly credits the interest on drawings, Rs. 15,500 ignores the opening credit balance, and calling the balance a credit balance reverses the sides.

stem: Uday's opening capital is Rs. 1,00,000. stem: Interest on drawings charged to partners is shown in the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account on the:
options: credit side, as it adds to the profit available
debit side, as it is an appropriation of profit
debit side, along with interest on capital
credit side, after the share of each partner
explanation: Correct option: (A). Interest on drawings is a gain to the firm, so it is credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account and increases the profit to be distributed. Interest on capital, salary and commission are the debit-side appropriations. It is not placed after the partners' shares; the shares are worked out only after it is added.

stem: Which journal entry transfers the salary allowed to a partner to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account?

Profit and Loss Appropriation A/c Dr. To Salary to Partner A/c
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. To Salary to Partner A/c

stem: Kunal and Lalit share profits 3:2. They admit Mira for a 1/5 share, and her guaranteed minimum profit of Rs. 60,000 is to be met by Kunal and Lalit in the ratio 2:3. Kunal and Lalit keep their old ratio between themselves. The firm's profit is Rs. 2,50,000. Lalit's final share of profit is:
explanation: Correct option: (D). Mira's share = 2,50,000 x 1/5 = Rs. 50,000; deficiency = Rs. 10,000. The remaining 2,00,000 goes 3:2, so Lalit gets 80,000. Lalit bears 3/5 of the deficiency under the agreed ratio 2:3 = Rs. 6,000. Lalit's final share = 80,000 - 6,000 = Rs. 74,000. Rs. 76,000 shares the deficiency in the old ratio 3:2 instead of the agreed ratio, Rs. 80,000 ignores the guarantee, and Rs. 70,000 makes Lalit bear the whole deficiency.

stem: Errors found after the final accounts are prepared and profits distributed are corrected, instead of altering old accounts, through:
options: a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account or the capital accounts
a revised Profit and Loss Account prepared for the earlier year
the Realisation Account opened in the books of the firm
the Revaluation Account opened in the books of the firm
explanation: Correct option: (A). The textbook states that, instead of altering old accounts, the adjustment is made either through a Profit and Loss Adjustment Account or directly in the capital accounts of the concerned partners. Old accounts are not redrawn. The Realisation Account is used on dissolution and the Revaluation Account on reconstitution of the firm.

stem: Which of the following situations calls for a past adjustment in partners' capital accounts?
options: A new partner is to be admitted into the firm at the start of next year
Interest on capital was not credited before profits were distributed
The firm bought new machinery for cash during the current accounting year
Partners agree to change their ratio from next year onwards
explanation: Correct option: (B). Past adjustments correct omissions or errors in earlier distribution of profit, such as interest on capital, interest on drawings, salary or commission left out. Admitting a partner or changing the ratio from next year are future events, not errors in past accounts. Buying machinery is an ordinary current transaction.

stem: Mona and Neel are equal partners with capitals of Rs. 80,000 and Rs. 40,000. After the accounts were closed, it was found that interest on capital at 10 per cent per annum had been omitted. The adjusting entry will be:
options: Mona's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 2,000 To Neel's Capital A/c Rs. 2,000
Neel's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 4,000 To Mona's Capital A/c Rs. 4,000
Neel's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 2,000 To Mona's Capital A/c Rs. 2,000
Profit and Loss A/c Dr. Rs. 12,000 To Partners' Capital A/cs Rs. 12,000
explanation: Correct option: (C). Interest due: Mona 8,000, Neel 4,000, total Rs. 12,000. This amount was wrongly distributed as profit equally: 6,000 each. Net effect: Mona short by 2,000 (8,000 - 6,000), Neel excess by 2,000 (6,000 - 4,000). So Neel is debited and Mona credited with Rs. 2,000. Reversing the entry makes the error worse, Rs. 4,000 is the difference in interest rather than the net effect, and debiting Profit and Loss Account would alter the closed accounts.

stem: Om and Pari share profits 3:2. After the accounts were closed, it was found that interest on drawings of Rs. 1,500 for Om and Rs. 500 for Pari had not been charged. The single adjusting entry will be:
options: Pari's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 300 To Om's Capital A/c Rs. 300
Om's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 1,000 To Pari's Capital A/c Rs. 1,000
Om's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 1,200 To Pari's Capital A/c Rs. 1,200
Om's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 300 To Pari's Capital A/c Rs. 300
explanation: Correct option: (D). Om and Pari should be debited 1,500 and 500 (total 2,000). That 2,000 would have increased the profit, credited 3:2: Om 1,200, Pari 800. Net: Om Dr. 300 (1,500 - 1,200); Pari Cr. 300 (800 - 500). So Om is debited and Pari credited with Rs. 300. Reversing the entry charges the wrong partner, Rs. 1,000 is the difference in interest, and Rs. 1,200 is only Om's share of the extra profit.

stem: Prem, Qasim and Ruhi share profits 2:2:1, with capitals of Rs. 1,00,000, Rs. 60,000 and Rs. 40,000. After the accounts were closed, it was found that interest on capital at 10 per cent per annum had been omitted. The adjusting entry will be:
options: Qasim's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 2,000 To Prem's Capital A/c Rs. 2,000
Prem's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 2,000 To Qasim's Capital A/c Rs. 2,000
Qasim's and Ruhi's Capital A/cs Dr. Rs. 1,000 each To Prem's Rs. 2,000
Ruhi's Capital A/c Dr. Rs. 2,000 To Prem's Capital A/c Rs. 2,000
explanation: Correct option: (A). Interest due: Prem 10,000, Qasim 6,000, Ruhi 4,000; total Rs. 20,000. This was distributed as profit 2:2:1: Prem 8,000, Qasim 8,000, Ruhi 4,000. Net: Prem short 2,000, Qasim excess 2,000, Ruhi nil. So Qasim is debited and Prem credited with Rs. 2,000. Ruhi is unaffected because her interest equals her share of the amount, so entries that debit Ruhi are wrong, and debiting Prem reverses the effect.
